items.title: QUIZ ON THE OVERWORKED PIECE
items.text:
161. Black moves. White’s Rook at c1 guards the other White Rook and the Bishop as well. What capture undermines the overworked piece?

162. Black moves. White’s Queen prevents mate at g2 and also guards the Knight at d3. What capture demonstrates that the White Queen is overworked?

163. White moves. Black’s Knight at c6 defends two pieces. How does White prove that this Knight is overworked?

164. Black’s Queen guards two pieces. How does White profit by this circumstance to win a piece at once?

NAPOLEON, who was a great general but only a mediocre chess player, coined the phrase “An army travels on its stomach” to emphasize the importance of supplying soldiers with food. Break the line of communications between soldiers and their food resources, and they are lost. On the chessboard we can think of the attacked piece as a soldier. When direct threats against it fail, we can aim our attack against its support. If we can destroy, drive off or exchange the guard of a piece, then we can win that piece.

items.title: BASIC PATTERN FOR REMOVING THE GUARD
items.text:
165. White moves. Black’s King is tied down to the defense of his Queen. If the King can be forced away, the Queen will be lost. The most forceful move is always a check or a capture. White plays 1 g7+! forcing the removal of the piece guarding the Queen. Black must play 1 ... xg7, whereupon 2 xe7+ is decisive.

166A. White moves. He sees that the vulnerable point in Black’s game is the Rook on d5, guarded only by the Black Queen. With White’s Queen and both Black Rooks in line, thoughts of a double attack suggest themselves. The guard must be removed! Therefore: 1 e7! This forces Black to abandon the protection of the Rook, with the continuation 1 ... xe7; 2 xd5+.

167A. Black moves. A little combination wins for Black, though he is behind in material: 1 ... d1+; 2 e1, c5.

He attacks the Queen which protects the Rook. White replies 3 a5, since the Queen must remain on the diagonal leading to the Rook.

168A. White moves. He can play 1 e4, attacking the Queen with his Knight, and meanwhile discovering attack on the Knight at f7 with his own Queen. But this would be pointless, as the Knight is guarded by the Black Bishop. “Is guarded by ...” – there is our clue! Remove the guard!

166B. Black moves. The double attack costs him his Rook at a8.

White’s task in 166A was to visualize the position with the guard (Black’s Queen) removed from the board. This led him to 1 e7 as the most forcible way to achieve his goal.

In chess you do not wait for things to happen – you make them happen. If not, things will happen to you.

167B. Black moves. He strikes at the Queen once more by 3 ... b6, and wins the Queen (and eventually the game) as the Queen must leave the vital diagonal.

168B. White moves. Now that the Black Knight at f7 has no protection, 2 xf7 wins easily.

Where pieces protect pieces, the mortality rate is high! The protecting piece is subject to exchange, capture or eviction. As pointed out in 167B, Pawns are more sturdy defenders; uprooting them is an expensive process.

169A. White moves. He can simplify with 1 xe8+, xe8; 2 xc7, e2+; 3 h3 etc., which is good enough. But he looks for a quick win, based on removing the guard. The indications are there, for the Black Rook, which can be captured with check, is guarded only by the Queen. White plays 1 g4+!

170A. Black moves. His pin on the Knight would normally yield dividends by the application of more pressure – say by ... e6. But he has no time, as his own Bishop is attacked. But there is a quicker course. The unhappy Knight is protected only by pieces. Therefore Black removes one of the guards with 1 ... xg2+.

171A. White moves. He has an open file for his King’s Rook, and simple doubling on this file would suffice to win (1 h5, g6; 2 ah1 etc.). But there is a quicker, more dynamic way, based on the fact that Black’s defensive force is scattered: 1 h7+! The Rook must be captured (if 1 ... g8? or 1 ... g6?; 2 xf7 mate).

169B. Black moves. To save his Queen he must play 1 ... xg4. Now White does not continue 2 fxg4? (which leaves him a Rook down after 2 ... xe1). Instead he continues as planned: 2 xe8+, now that the Rook’s defender has been removed. Black has no time to save his Queen (priority of check!). After 2 ... g7; 3 fxg4 wins easily.

170B. White moves. His reply is forced: 2 xg2. Now that White’s Knight has lost a vital prop, Black has a winning double attack: 2 ... xe4+ (2 ... xe4+ is also good); 3 xe4, xe4+ followed by 4 ... xb1. An inventory of the final position shows Black to be a piece ahead, with an easy win. The winning method here is of great practical value.

171B. Black moves. As we have shown, 1 ... xh7 is forced. But now White has removed the only defender (the Black King!) of the f-Pawn, or, more exactly, of the square f7. After 2 xf7+, Black has 2 ... h8 or 2 ... h6; in either event 3 h1+ puts Black out of his misery. In this case, removing the guard led to a mating attack.

172A. White moves. He attacks the hostile Knight twice. It is defended twice. Both guards are pieces. If either defender can be captured or driven off, the Knight will be lost – his guard will be removed. These reflections lead logically to 1 b6, which forks both guards: the Rook and Bishop.

173A. Black moves. His Rook attacks White’s Knight, which is defended by a Bishop. Remove this guard and White’s position collapses. As in 172A, a Knight fork does the trick: 1 ... c4. The menaced Rook must stay on the second rank to guard the Bishop, hence 2 c2. Black is well on the way to achieving his objective.

174A. White moves. He sees that the position of the hostile Knight is shaky. It has two defenders – but both can be knocked out. How? Not by 1 xd6?, cxd6; 2 dxe5, dxe5 and the Knight is guarded by a sturdy Pawn. We need a more accurate order of moves: 1 dxe5!, xe5 (if 1 ... xe5; 2 xf4 wins a piece). Now to remove a guard.

172B. Black moves. He plays 1 ... b8. This is inadequate, but he has nothing better. Now there follows 2 xa8, xa8 and, amusingly enough, neither of the Black Knight’s guards is functioning. White now captures the Knight, with a piece ahead. Maxim: Knock out the prop, and the piece falls!

173B. Black moves. Has he really come nearer to his goal? He has blocked the action of his own Rook, and even permitted White to increase the Knight’s protection. But, as has been pointed out, pieces are unstable guards. Now comes 2 ... xb2; 3 xb2. Both defenders are gone; 3 ... xc3 wins the piece after all. An impressive example because of its simplicity.

174B. White moves. With the Knight guarded by two pieces, the rest is easy: remove one of the guards. The move we want is 2 xd6, and whichever way Black recaptures, we continue with 3 xf4. The way in which White proves that the Knight is inadequately defended is genuinely instructive.

175A. White moves. His attack is concentrated against the pinned Knight. He can remove the guard (the King) by 1 h8+, but after 1 ... xh8; 2 xg6 he has lost material: the Knight is less valuable than the sacrificed Rook. But try a different order of moves: 1 xg6+ xg6.

176A. White moves. Our familiarity with removing the guard suggests that Black’s Queen, being defended by only the Knight, is in difficulties. But we must force Black’s hand, else he escapes by ... xd2+. What we need is a forcing move which reduces Black’s choice of a reply; we look for a capture or a check. Therefore: 1 e7+.

177A. White moves. His Rook menaces Black’s Bishop, which is guarded by his Knight, which in turn is guarded by a Pawn. To remove the guard, it is necessary to “destroy the house that Jack built” by removing the Pawn that guards the Knight that guards the Bishop.

175B. White moves. He has forced a position where the pinned piece (the Queen) is of greater value than the sacrificial Rook. Now 2 h8+ is successful, for it forcibly tears away Black’s King from the defense of his Queen. After 2 ... xh8; 3 xg6 White has an easy win.

176B. Black moves. If 1 ... xe7, the Queen’s guard is removed, allowing 2 xd4. Therefore Black must play 1 ... d8 or 1 ... b8. The problem is still “Delenda est Carthago!” – remove the guard! We accomplish this with another check (priority of check!) by playing 2 xc6+. Now Black’s defense topples. White will play 3 xd4.

177B. White moves. He has knocked out the props from under the Knight and can now repeat the process by 2 xb3. After 2 ... xb3, White removes the defenseless Bishop by 3 xd4.

White’s method of winning the Bishop is best described as “removing the guard of the guard.”

178A. Black moves. He sees that the weak link in his opponent’s game is the Bishop. This piece is guarded only by means of other pieces. Black removes the guard by 1 ... xc3, forcing 2 bxc3. White’s defense is about to collapse.

178B. Black moves. He has knocked out one guard. The Pawn push 2 ... g5 disposes of the remaining guard. White has the sad choice of moving the Knight and losing the Bishop, or of saving the Bishop and losing the Knight.

179A. White moves. He is a piece down, but can regain it with 1 xe4+, xe4; 2 e5+ etc. But he wants something more forceful. White works out a daring idea by removing the guard: 1 xc5!!, xf3.

179B. White moves. He must justify his Queen sacrifice. He continues his plan: 2 e1+. This forces 2 ... e7 (interposing the Queen is useless). Now comes 3 xe7+, f8; 4 d8 mate.

items.title: QUIZ ON REMOVING THE GUARD
items.text:
180. White moves. His Queen, now unprotected, attacks Black’s Queen, which is protected. Has White time to remove the guard? How?

181. White moves. Instead of retreating his menaced Knight, he finds a way to remove the guard from the Black Rook which he attacks. How?

182. Black moves. How does he win the Queen by removing its guard?

183. Black moves. How does he win the Queen by removing its guard?

IN CHESS, we must always strive to give our pieces freedom of action. A piece that is not free to go to other squares has no mobility – no freedom of action – and is often in danger of being lost. An attack on it is frequently successful, for the trapped piece has lost the option of fleeing: it has no retreat. In its paralyzed state, it is helpless against the well aimed thrusts of hostile pieces.

One reason why we are constantly admonished to “centralize” pieces is that pieces occupying the center have much more scope for action than have pieces posted at the side of the board. This is particularly true of the Knight.

Yet centralization must not be an automatic process. A piece in the very center of the board whose activity is hampered by its fellowpieces, is exposed to the threat of attack and capture. As for pieces at the side of the board, their mortality rate is frightful!

items.title: 184. Black moves. He has an easy victim in White’s Knight at the side of the board. This piece has no retreat. But how should the Knight’s awkward situation be exploited? Should Black attack it with his Queen by 1 ... e8? No, for after 2 g3 the Knight would be protected.
items.text: The right way is the Pawn stab 1 ... g5! winning the Knight. Against a Pawn’s attack on a piece, neither exchange nor protection can be satisfactory.
